Test: `ladder::products_whose_factors_one_sum_on_the_factors_joins_scale`, 8 → 64 links: 9.2 times the instructions (109.2M → 999.7M) and 7.5 times the bytes, against the limit 17.6; the variant with the sum over `w{i} == b{i}` 9.7 times. Negative control on main, run once and not committed: 35.8 times the bytes, failed. Not proved: that the rule loses no proof the products of every pair give; a loss needs `u * v` cancelled through the product of two premises on another pair of factors. Remaining cost: the test of one premise against `y` costs, for each factor it passes, the rows on that factor; on the family the first factor of the sum other than `x` is foreign and the test stops there, but many long rows sharing factors that are not foreign can make it O(n²); not measured on any family. Still quadratic in `Tier::Local`: one large biconnected block with many open sides, which is an integer program per side (NP-hard; no way is known to share one side's search with another's, and `project_each` also hulls each symbol on its own; not proved that none exists). Not fixed: the projection's per-symbol `hull_from` for a group with a general row (`project_parts`) has the same per-symbol shape, not measured here. A top-level `||` premise joins the part of its atoms like any other row (`products` puts it in `joined` with the negations) and gives them bounds through the widest over its disjuncts (`disjunction_bounds`); only a disjunction inside a disjunct is not read. Names (coordinator review, 2026-11-09): `eliminate` ties each atom to its nearest factor by the shortest-path search, and that search broke ties of distance by the order of the factors, which is the order of their names, so renaming the variables could change which bounds were found (`(v >= 0 && c >= 0 && u >= w1 && u >= w2 && v >= w1 && v >= w2 + 1 && w1 + w2 >= 10 && (w1 >= -1000 || w2 <= -2000))` to `u * c >= 5 * c && v * c >= 0` was proved from `u >= 5` alone, and from `u >= 5` and `v >= 6` with the names reversed); now an atom that two factors reach at the same least distance, or that is reached only through such an atom, is tied to neither and counts with its own bound, so the answer cannot depend on names (`Differences::search`: each node is taken from the heap at most twice, once with one nearest factor and once with none, so the cost stays O(m log n)). Keeping the bound of every tied path (their meet) was not taken: it costs O(rows × tied factors), quadratic on a hub `w <= f_i` for n factors with many rows on `w`. Test: `ladder::the_bounds_found_do_not_depend_on_names` checks every family in the ladder tests that goes through the search, and four cases with two tied paths that give different bounds, under the reversed name order and a rotation, for the same verdict and the same certificate up to the renaming; it fails on 2d6a2c67 C2-pairs-exact (2026-11-12): the foreign-factor rule above lost proofs that cancel a product atom through the products of another pair of factors: from `-c >= 0`, `1 - a - d >= 0`, `1 + a - b + c >= 0`, `-a - c >= 0`, `b - a >= 0`, `-a - b - d >= 0`, the goal `1 + a * b - b - b * b + b * c + c + c * c - d >= 0` needs `(-a - b - d) * (-c)`, a product for `b * c`, whose atom `c * d` cancels against `(1 - a - d) * (1 + a - b + c)`, a product for `a * b`; the rule left `-a - b - d` out for `b * c` since `d` is foreign to `c`, and the goal was not proved (`ladder::a_product_atom_cancels_through_the_products_of_another_pair`, fails on f0ce6ac5e). A Python model of both rules found 4 such losses in 72,000 random entailments; this is the one of them that the Rust code also lost (the other three are proved there through the bound rows of the factors). Now a product is left out exactly when it alone, among the products not yet left out, holds an atom that no premise, goal or definition mentions, with a nonzero coefficient, to a fixpoint (`presburger::pairs::kept`). That changes no verdict of the linear reading: the atom can take a value of the sign of its coefficient large enough for its one product, and the products left out are justified in the reverse of the order they go; the rule is monotone, so the products kept depend neither on order nor on names. A pair `{p, q}`, `|q| <= |p|`, is tested from its factor rows without expanding the product: for each `w` of `q`, the `z` of `p` with `w * z` mentioned, cancelled inside `p ⊗ q`, or held by another live pair (read from the pairs on the rows holding `w`; a pair `{r, p}` with `r` holding `w` and `p` not holding it holds every `w * z`) are collected, and the pair goes when they are fewer than the variables of `p`. A worklist retests a pair only when a pair that held one of its atoms at its last test goes. The naive method, expanding every product and counting the holders of each atom after each round, costs O(rounds × Σ |p| × |q|), Θ(k²) on the family. Tests: `presburger::pairs::tests::the_pairs_kept_are_those_left_by_expanding_every_product` (4,000 random cases against that naive method, the pairs in random order); `ladder::products_whose_factors_one_sum_on_the_factors_joins_scale` 8 → 64: 8.8 times the instructions (62.2M → 549.4M) and 7.2 times the bytes, where the rule of f0ce6ac5e took 9.2 times (109.7M → 1,005.5M); `..._one_sum_joins_scale` 9.5 times (124.2M → 1,178.8M); `products_whose_premise_holds_k_atoms_in_no_product_scale` 8.7 times (4.2M → 36.7M); limit 17.6, load 34 to 45. Negative controls, run once and not committed: every product kept, 21.2 and 34.0 times the bytes on the first and third, failed; no retest after a drop, the random test fails at its first case. A variant that also leaves out a product whose free atom every other live holder holds with the same sign is exact by the same argument; on 18,000 random entailments it proved the same goals, and the solver's refusals (a name tie or growth) moved in both directions (702 against 705, 981 against 972), so it was not taken. Remaining cost: the test of a pair reads, for each variable `w` of the shorter row, the pairs on the rows holding `w`, O(min(|s|, |p|) × log) for each, so many long rows that share variables cost more than O(n log n); no bound better than the products themselves is known for that case, and no family of it has been measured. The pairs themselves are still Σ over the products of |rows on x| × |rows on y|, Θ(n²) for n rows on each of two factors. |

Failing (measured, UTVPI-NEAR repair): BAD-GOR augmented joined with a fan (a path of weight -1 edges into a hub fanning out to k leaves, which makes BF-Dijkstra take k rounds of k work) makes both quick searches quadratic while they are still cheaper than Duong's, so the race takes 201.9M → 12,236M instructions from k = 256 to 2,048, 60.6 times, past the limit of 24 (`l01_38_presburger::stages::bad_gor_and_a_fan_scale`, ignored); alone, Goldberg and Radzik 80.8M → 4,699M (58.2 times), BF-Dijkstra 62.3M → 3,708M (59.5 times), Duong 1,176M → 14,070M (12.0 times). In units of work, Goldberg and Radzik 546k → 33.4M, BF-Dijkstra 344k → 19.3M, Duong 3.72M → 43.1M and 404M at k = 16,384; the race is at most three times the cheapest in units, so asymptotically Duong's bound holds, but the crossover lies past k = 2,048. Starting each merge's BF-Dijkstra from the copies of the tails of negative edges only cut Duong's cost on this family from 1,880M to 1,176M at k = 256; passing would need about 2.7 units per edge per scaling step against about 14 now and about 1 for the pass over the edges alone, so a cut in this constant cannot pass it; a near-linear search with a small constant is needed (open: item UTVPI-union). Main before UTVPI-NEAR (Goldberg and Radzik alone, not resumable) takes 53.3M → 2,993M on this family, 56.2 times: quadratic as well, and about 4 times cheaper at both sizes, since the race does at least one unit of each search per unit of the one that finishes (measured at load 76–82, UTVPI-NEAR repair 2). Duong's figures on BAD-GOR alone (0.91G, 11.5G) predate that change. **Ruling (orchestrator, 2026-11-03 12:21, after UTVPI-NEAR verify 2):** the gap on this family is accepted for the merge. The race costs about 4 times main: main 53.3M → 2,993M, the race 202.3M → 12,236M (both measured in repair 2), so main grows 56.2 times and the race 60.5 times, the same growth, and both fail the limit of 24. The extra cost is a constant bounded by the number of racers: the race does at most one unit of each of its three searches per unit of the one that finishes, and Goldberg and Radzik's search made resumable costs 80.8M against main's 53.3M at k = 256. In exchange BAD-GOR passes (main 59.7 times there, the race 7.8). The fix belongs to item UTVPI-union. **UTVPI-union (2026-11-05): fixed; every family below is 8.0 to 8.7 times from k = 256 to 2,048, in instructions (load 55 to 77).** (1) Split by strongly connected components (Tarjan, `components`, now shared with `odd_zero_cycle`), each component searched alone, then the components in topological order, each shifted by the least of `bound[v] − q[v]` over its nodes, where `bound[v]` is the least of 0 and `p[u] + w` over edges into `v` from earlier components; this replaces the Kahn pass and decides a graph with no cycle in O(V + E). On `bad_gor_and_a_fan_scale` (BAD-GOR and the fan share no variable) it alone gives 35.6M → 284M, 8.0 times. (2) Condensation does not fix the connected variant: with heavy edges both ways between the halves and a heavy ring on the fan (each fan node to the next two, weight n², so fill > 0), the halves are one component of the positive literals, but the half slow for Goldberg and Radzik and the half slow for BF-Dijkstra fall in opposite signs of the literal graph (a row `x[u] − x[v] + w ≥ 0` is the edge `2u → 2v` and the reversed edge `2v+1 → 2u+1`), so the split still separates the slow parts and that variant passes at 8.1 times. With the fan's edges reversed as well (`union_family(k, true, true)`), both slow parts share one component, and the old race on it takes 459k → 25.9M units, 56 times, won by Duong's search at k = 2,048. (3) `Shared`: Goldberg and Radzik's search, at the start of each pass, takes the labels BF-Dijkstra lowered; BF-Dijkstra, at the end of each round, takes those Goldberg and Radzik lowered. Proved: every label is the weight of a walk from the source; pass i of Goldberg and Radzik leaves each label at most the shortest path of i edges, and round i of BF-Dijkstra at most the shortest walk with i negative edges, both monotone under extra decreases, so the n-pass and V-round tests for a negative cycle and Goldberg and Radzik's cycle test stay sound; a label taken mid-round would be skipped if its node was settled, hence the round boundary. On the joined, reversed family the race takes 38.1M → 332.8M, 8.7 times (`the_joined_union_family_scales`); through `decide`, `the_joined_union_family_scales_through_decide` (the old code 618M → 18,351M, 29.7 times). Other families: the fan reversed, not joined, 39.7M → 329.9M (8.3); `bad_gor_and_a_fan_scale` 36.1M → 301.2M (8.3); BAD-GOR alone 25.1M → 209.3M (8.3); the acyclic family 5.29M → 42.3M (8.0). (4) The wide-row variant (a fresh unit variable `y` in `y + x[0] − x[a] ≥ 0`): `decide` drops `y` as bounded on one side only, and the halves reach the search apart, so it passed on the old code too (421M → 3,852M, 9.1 times, the same as unjoined); `the_wide_row_family_scales_through_decide` and `the_union_family_scales_through_decide` stay as tests. Candidates, scored 0 to 10: split and `Shared` together, all families 8.0 to 8.7 times, 10 (kept); `Shared` alone, all families pass but the acyclic family costs 20.1M → 166.4M, 3.8 times the split, 7; split alone, the joined reversed family 56 times, 2; a cut in Duong's constant, rejected in UTVPI-NEAR repair (about 2.7 units per edge per step needed, about 14 measured), 1; BCF, below, 1. **BCF rejected** (Bringmann, Cassis and Fischer, "Negative-Weight Single-Source Shortest Paths in Near-Linear Time: Now Faster!", FOCS 2023; arXiv 2304.05279, checked against its LaTeX source in UTVPI-union verify: a Las Vegas algorithm in O((E + V·log log V)·log²V·log(V·W)) time "with high probability (and in expectation)" (Theorem 1.1), O(E·log²V·log(V·W)·log log V) in its abstract): (a) its bound is expected time over random choices; DESIGN's rule on low complexity (DESIGN.md, "Every algorithm is of low complexity") admits randomness only as a last resort at points derived from content, and with a seed derived from the input the bound is no longer an expectation over that input, so a family can be slow for its fixed seed (inferred); (b) a deterministic near-linear search, Duong's, already gives the asymptotic bound in the race; (c) it is built on the same scaling and low-diameter decomposition as Duong's, so its constant is likely of the same order, which is what made Duong's search lose below k = 2,048 (inferred, not measured); (d) no measured family needs it. A family slow for both Goldberg and Radzik and BF-Dijkstra along the same shortest paths, constructed in UTVPI-union verify: `split_bad_gor`, BAD-GOR with each weight 1 edge of its path split into edges of weight -1 and 2. From k = 256 to 2,048 in time (load 65 to 73), Goldberg and Radzik alone grows 232 times, BF-Dijkstra alone 131 times, Duong alone 223 ms to 7.27 s, and the race 432 ms to 33.8 s (78 times, 1.9 and 4.6 times Duong alone); from k = 128 to 1,024 the race allocates 33.5 times the bytes, past the limit 24, while Duong alone passes. The guess that the labels BF-Dijkstra passes slow Goldberg and Radzik down was wrong (UTVPI-both-slow, in instructions from k = 128 to 1,024, load 58 to 68): Goldberg and Radzik alone 32.7M → 1,694M (51.8 times, 127 and 1,024 passes), BF-Dijkstra alone 46.6M → 2,826M (60.7 times), `Shared` 98.2M → 5,943M (60.5 times; labels passed one way only, 56.5 and 58.2 times; not passed, 57.3 times, but then `the_joined_union_family_scales` takes 287M → 16.5G), Duong alone 535M → 6,218M (11.6 times), the race 175M → 9,778M (55.9 times): both quick searches are quadratic on this family by themselves. **UTVPI-both-slow (2026-11-05): fixed.** The reverse of a graph has the potential `-q` for each potential `q` of the graph and the same cycles; on the reverse of `split_bad_gor` both quick searches are fast, so a second `Shared` on the reversed graph joins the race (`utvpi::race`, with `reversed` and `negated`), one step after each unit of Duong's search. `stages::split_bad_gor_scales` passes: 24.2M → 198M, 8.2 times (bytes 3.90M → 31.6M, 8.1 times); `the_joined_union_family_scales` 50.9M → 411M (8.1), `bad_gor_and_a_fan_scale` 40.7M → 324M (8.0), `bad_gor_scales` 26.5M → 206M (7.8). The differential test runs `Shared` on the reverse, negated, against Bellman–Ford on 6,000 random graphs; a mutant without the negation fails three unit tests. Negative control, run once and not committed: with the reverse pair disabled `split_bad_gor_scales` fails at 32.4 times the bytes (18.9M → 612M; load 39 to 50). Fixed by UTVPI-both-ways (decision A17, option A: a smaller constant in Duong's search): `split_bad_gor_both_ways`, the family beside its reverse in one component, is slow for both pairs, so Duong's search finishes first; the race took 385M → 30,322M instructions (78.7 times, 51.2 times the bytes; load 39 to 54) and now takes 445M → 9,425M (21.2 times, 17.2 times the bytes; load 11 to 21), `stages::split_bad_gor_both_ways_scales`, un-ignored. In `negsssp::Solver::run`, measured by switching each change off: (1) each step first runs BF-Dijkstra on `c` with one unit per edge (`Solver::quick`) until it first runs out (26.7 times without it; 21.4 with all four, in the probe build); (2) after a decomposition, padded balls are peeled off the rest of the set ([D] Lemma padding composition, `Solver::peel`), which took the vertices decomposed from 337K to 162K (31.3 times without it); (3) the next potential is `phi + 2·psi` when that leaves the least reduced weight higher, 27 steps to 16 (fails without it); (4) the negative edges of `c` are kept in compressed rows, so the scan for a negative edge inside a set and BF-Dijkstra's rounds visit only them (23.3 times without). The per-step build of `c` takes one unit per vertex and per negative edge: a unit per edge gave 24.9 times, and none made each unit of Duong's search dearer, the race up to 5% slower on the quick families. The 21.2 times from 128 to 1,024 is the crossover the model above gives, not the growth of Duong's search. Inferred from a model, not measured: with the quick searches quadratic and Duong's linear on a family, and Duong's search first to finish from size k* on, the race grows about 8·k*/k times from k to 8k for k*/8 ≤ k ≤ k*, past 24 for k < k*/3, whatever quick searches race; only a smaller constant in Duong's search moves such families under the limit. Duong's search now publishes an estimate of the units it will do in all (`negsssp::Progress`: units done, plus the steps left, at most `⌈log₂ need⌉`, times the dearest step of the recursion so far, plus `n + 2m` for the final Dijkstra search), once a step has used the recursion; the pairs take no step while their units exceed the units it has still to do, and resume if the estimate rises. The estimate is about twice the units done in the end (1.95M units into the 12,284-vertex component at k = 1,024: estimate 14.0M, end 6.7M), since the bound on the steps left is loose. | C-WIDEN | `check::widen`, the intervals of the widening warning | intervals come from literals, the operators, names bound by `=` and the joins of `if`, `else` and blocks, with no narrowing by a test and no relation between operands: a parameter, a call or a value a test bounds is any `int`, and its operations are not reported; `x - x` with `x` in `int[lo..=hi]` gets `int[lo - hi..=hi - lo]`, and is reported when that interval leaves the word though the value is 0 | narrowing by tests needs the facts on each path and relating operands needs a relational domain, whose cost per operation grows with the number of names in scope (exponential in the worst case for Presburger formulas), where an interval costs O(1); the store's forward transfer over the definition graph, which narrows by tests and relations, is the complete reading and replaces this walk at step L1.40b; until then a linear walk gives the warning for the common case of large literals | a parameter in an operation; `x - x` with `x` near the ends of the word. `l01_29_diagnostics::widen::a_parameter_is_not_bounded_and_does_not_warn`, `a_difference_of_a_value_with_itself_is_read_as_a_range` |
| C25 | `store/interval.rs` `bit_word` (steps L1.39a, L1.39f) | each operand of a bit word but the `x` of `shl` and `shr` is read by its hull, and the result is at most two intervals, so a hole in an operand is lost and `bitAnd`, `bitOr` and `bitXor` are bounded by their operands' digits, not by the digits they share; `f64Bits` is `int[0..]`, since `2^64` is past `i64`; the machine operations of step L1.39f are bounded by their width (`mulHi` by the product of the corners as well, `bitReverse`, `byteSwap`) or by one operand's upper end (`pdep` by `mask`, `pext` by `x` and the digits of `mask`), and DESIGN gives the funnel shifts no bound, so they take the hull `0 ..< 2^w` | the words are not monotone, so the exact image of a union of pieces is a search over the pieces' digits; the hull rule is O(1) per word, and `shl` and `shr`, monotone on each sign, map each piece of `x` by its corners in O(pieces) | an operand of more than one piece, or `bitAnd`, `bitOr`, `bitXor` on operands of more than one value. `l01_39a_bit_words::transfer` (soundness on 100,000 random sets of intervals) and `l01_39f_int_machine_ops::transfer` (soundness on 70,000 random tuples of intervals at widths up to 127); the known-bits domain of step L1.40a is the complete solution |
| C26 | `check/mod.rs` `Ck::known`, `check/arms.rs` (steps L1.39a, NARROW-if) | an operand's domain is decided from its text (literals, names bound to such text, `+ - * div mod ^`, the bit words) and its listed values, met with the scope of the reduced product that the tests around it make (`Ck::ints_here`: the arms of `if` and `else if`, the second side of `&&` and `\|\|`, `!`), not from the reduced product's cell after the store's fixpoint, so an int that comes from a caller or the input and that no test bounds is rejected as possibly negative, as `^`'s exponent is; a test on a call or field is an opaque value of its own span, so it says nothing of a second, equal call | the checker runs before the store's iteration; asking the store at each call would run a fixpoint per call, where reading the text is O(1) per node, each node read once, children before parents on an explicit stack, and a binder's value read only when a bit word or an exponent reads its name; each test's scope is its parent's narrowed by that test, computed once on first read and kept, so `k` nested tests or `k` sides of `&&` cost `k` narrowings; a case no state reaches (the failing case of `a >= i \|\| a >= i + 3`, the else arm of a failing `&&`) keeps its names with `bottom` set (`Scope::assume_case`, `Scope::get` gives the bottom for each), so it costs its test and not the names in scope: before this (repair 2 of NARROW-if) a nest of `k` such tests on `k` names emptied every name at each level, 1.03 s and 94 MB at `k` = 400 against 6.05 s and 1056 MB at 1600, now 0.52 s 41 MB against 2.01 s 135 MB. A name bound before the test is not narrowed by it (`k = n - 1; if n > 0 { popCount(k) }` is rejected), since a binder is read in the scope it was bound under, as DESIGN.md binds it; relating `k` to `n` needs the linear relations of the store (S15) in the checker. A rejection under tests names only the tests that bear on its operand (`Arms::deciding`): a test that changed the product of a name the operand reads (`Arms::lookup`, below), or of a name the value of a binder it reads reads, looked up from the node the binder was bound under; from such a test, unless the test alone gives the name its product there (`Arms::explains`, one narrowing of the test on a scope of its own names), the lookup goes on above it for each name of the test; and a test that changed a name it does not read (through the scope's relation) brings in the tests of one shortest path of the relation from that name to a name the test reads: a breadth-first search over the tests above it from the names it reads, each name keeping the test that reached it (`Arms::carried`, one search per such test, kept and resumed by later lookups, so each test above is expanded once per name it reads). Each node keeps, once a rejection under it needs it, a persistent map from each name to the nearest node that reads it (`Arms::chains`; a join maps the names its two sides map differently, found by the maps' difference as `Scope::join` finds its names), and the nearest test that changed a name's settled product is found up skew-binary jump pointers (`Arms::add`, `Arms::step`; products only narrow along a chain of tests, so a jump to a node with the same product skips no change), each answer kept per node and name (`Arms::lookup`), so a rejection costs O(log n) per test it names, not the tests around it. Whether a hub admits a leaf is kept in O(log n) per change: each hub of such a leaf counts the names its free conjuncts mention, and each leaf how many of them are its hubs (`StarIndex::near`, `hits`, `level`). When no shortest path gives the name its product, alone or from the other names' products, the longer paths are searched (`Arms::longer`): under `x <= n + 100`, `y >= n`, `x >= y`, then `n >= -1`, the notes named `x <= n + 100`, which gives `x` no bound, and neither test that does; they now name `y >= n` and `x >= y`. Before, each step of a derivation printed its type alone and each print walked the whole graph of the type, so n steps over types that share n levels cost O(n²) in time and allocation for a text of O(n). Now the table of a message's definitions keeps each part a step printed, with its name or text, keyed by the part and the two printing flags; a later step of the same message takes the part from the table instead of printing it again, so each part is printed once per message, O(m log m) for m parts. A part is kept only when every part inside it was printed the same way in that step (`Printer::remember`), so a part named in one step and written out in another is printed again. A step whose type holds a union or intersection beside a part taken from the table is printed anew whole, since the order of a union's members follows their texts: one more print of that step. A part holding a union or intersection, which is named by the uses of the whole type, was not kept, so a chain whose every link holds a union stayed O(n²); since MSG-derive-print-unions such a part is kept with the uses of the unions inside it and taken again where the later type uses them alike (row K110). A part that holds a value the program writes in two ways (`0x1F` and `31`, `-0r` and `0r`) is not kept, since each step writes the value as its own line does (`Spelled::everywhere`), and the table is cleared when the spellings change (`Ck::spells` → `forget_printed`) | One batch print per message with use counts kept per step (the other option of the brief) was rejected by analysis, without a prototype: a count per step needs the parts of each step, which is the O(n²) walk again, and ranking `T1`, `T2`, … over one print of all steps changes the expected texts. Taken: predict the time from the operands' sizes in units fitted once, so the verdict is the same on every machine (deterministic checking) and the limit is close to 250 ms here. Cost: the prediction is one pass over each operand, already paid by the operation it charges. Spread: the fixed per-law overhead (reading the law, the two points, hashing; about 70 to 140 µs plus about 200 ns per unit of size) is not charged, so laws under a millisecond take up to about 2.5 times their prediction; families above 10 ms are within 0.57 to 1.55 times (load 66; the gapped square, 0.57, is the one below 0.7). Since POLY-crossover-bench the method of each product is chosen by constants fitted to instructions (Crossovers, POLY-nf), which makes the small products of `(x + y) ^ 72 - x` dense: charged as before, it took 2.1 to 2.4 times its prediction (7,924 units with the dense fixed cost charged, 4,153 without, 10,590 before); `LIMIT` measured again on 2026-11-13 at load 45 to 55 (three runs each): the product law at 1000, 2,114,040 units, 30.2 ms predicted, 32.2 to 36.8 ms taken (1.07 to 1.22); the split at 72, 0.113 ms predicted, 0.110 to 0.132 ms (0.97 to 1.16); the split at 4096, 13,934,777 units, 199 ms predicted, 161 to 196 ms (0.81 to 0.99). The ratios are those of before (1.08 to 1.11, 1.17 to 1.21, 0.74 to 0.75), so `LIMIT` stays 17,500,000. So a refusal costs at most the limit, and a proof at most twice it (the factored path has its own budget and gives way to the expansion when it passes it). Corpus (`l03_09_egraph::measure`, 32 obligations): each costs less than a thousandth of the limit | `poly::tests::refused_shapes` (a product of three powers past the limit, with the full message; its false variant refuted; `(x + y) ^ 1000` split proved; the work of `a + c == c + a` and `x == x`), `poly::tests::products_of_powers`, `poly::tests::the_charges_are_the_measured_ones` (a sum chain of 1 to 40 names and a product of two sums of 20 names, charged exactly as the constants say), `l03_09_egraph::refusal` (the full message on `(1 + x) ^ 1024 * (1 + y) ^ 1024 - x`, refused within a twentieth of the limit; the split proved at 128 and 1024), `l03_09_egraph::factored::the_a98_laws_at_exponent_1000` (proved at 10 and 1000, refused at 2^32 within the limit), `l03_09_egraph::calibration` (the three timings above, each within 2x), `l03_09_egraph::scaling::a_sum_of_n_monomials_in_n_names` (n = 1000 and 8000, listed keys, sums only: 61.2 M and 552.4 M instructions, 9.03 times; 7.5 MB and 64.8 MB, 8.6 times; limit 13). ## Crossovers

A crossover is a size at which code changes from one method to another that gives an
identical result, so nothing observable changes there. DESIGN P9 asks for the crossing to be
solved from the two methods' cost formulas, with the target's constants as parameters. The
author accepted crossovers set from timings for now (2026-11-06), on these conditions:
- the two methods' results are identical, and a test compares them;
- each crossover is commented at its site with the timings it rests on, their date and the
  load average;
- the timings are measured again when the code is rewritten in Zed for self-hosting (row S),
  when the cost characteristics and the anomalies below are to be understood more fully;
- where one method is never slower than the other, it is used alone, with no crossover.

### NUM-subquad, `zed-kernel/src/num/fast.rs`, measured 2026-11-06

Procedure (the test was not committed): a release test build of `zed-kernel`, load average 1.0
to 1.4, each method repeated at each size until 40 ms had passed, on random dense operands
with the top bit set. Multiplication: `transform_mul` of two `w`-word factors against
num-bigint's `*`. Division: `div_rem` of `2w` by `w` words against num-bigint's `div_rem`.
Gcd: `gcd` of two `w`-word numbers against num-bigint's. Printing: `to_decimal` against
`to_str_radix(10)`. For the run the test-build leaves were changed: `DIV_LEAF` to 4 words and
`RECIP_LEAF` to 2, so that Newton division runs below its leaf, and `MUL_LEAF` to the build's
1024. With its test value 48, the products inside division, gcd and printing use the transform
from 48 words, which raises the gcd's ratio at 1024 words from 0.50 to 0.64. `GCD_LEAF` kept
its test value of 16 words. Each entry is NUM-subquad's time over num-bigint's at the same
size; below 1 NUM-subquad is faster.

| Operation (leaf in the build) | Ratio at each size in words |
|---|---|
| multiplication (1024) | 64: 6.20, 128: 3.96, 256: 2.69, 512: 2.03, 768: 2.23, 1024: 1.50, 1536: 1.80, 2048: 1.18, 4096: 0.96, 8192: 0.73, 16384: 0.56 |
| division, `2w` by `w` (64) | 8: 2.13, 16: 1.66, 32: 1.25, 64: 1.13, 96: 1.00, 128: 1.06, 256: 1.28, 512: 1.60, 1024: 2.03, 2048: 3.84, 4096: 3.28, 8192: 2.60 |
| gcd (512) | 64: 2.44, 128: 1.80, 256: 1.20, 384: 0.76, 512: 0.78, 768: 0.51, 1024: 0.50, 2048: 0.34, 4096: 0.24, 8192: 0.17 |
| printing (1024 digits, about 53 words) | 64: 0.94, 256: 0.93, 1024: 1.01, 4096: 1.46, 16384: 1.74, 32768: 1.50, 65536: 1.27, 131072: 0.96 |

What the curves show, and what is not yet understood:
- Each method's own curve is smooth; a leaf only chooses between two curves. A scaling test
  whose `n` lies below a leaf and whose `8n` lies above it measures the change of curve, not
  either method: `reading_a_rat_of_two_wide_parts_scales` at 2,500 digits grew 75 times in
  bytes across the gcd's leaf (K41).
- Multiplication crosses near 4096 words, not at the leaf of 1024; from 1024 to 4096 words the
  build takes up to 1.5 times the faster method's time. The transform's time rises in steps
  with its padded length: 512 to 768 words multiplies it by 2.08, 768 to 1024 by 1.03, 1024
  to 1536 by 2.18, 1536 to 2048 by 1.04. BIGINT-fast-mul (below) made the transform 1.5 to 2
  times faster, lowered the leaf to 512 and put a cost decision above it.
- The gcd crosses near 300 words, below the leaf of 512; from 300 to 512 words the build takes
  up to 1.3 times the faster method's time. Across 1024 to 8192 words num-bigint's Stein gcd
  grows 59 times (about `n^2`) and the half gcd 20 times.
- Newton division is never faster up to 8192 words. Its ratio peaks at 3.84 at 2048 words and
  falls about 0.8 times each doubling after that, so the curves would cross above 100,000 words
  (extrapolated, not measured). The cause of the excess is not measured; candidates are the
  full product `a2 y` of which only the high half is used, the product `q b` in `settle`, and a
  reciprocal built at each call. KERNEL-div-newton (2026-11-09, load 15 to 17) replaced it:
  the division by `Level` takes 1.31 times num-bigint's time at 96 words, 2.54 at 1024, 1.88
  at 2048, 1.36 at 4096, 1.02 at 8192, 0.76 at 16,384 and 0.46 at 65,536, for `2w` by `w`.
  The curves now cross near 8192 words; `DIV_LEAF` stays at 64 words, so from 64 to 8192 words
  the division takes up to 2.5 times the faster method's time. Not moved, as a move needs the
  cost model `newton_cost` to be measured against these times first (follow-up
  DIV-crossover-model).
- The remainder tree of `zedc_int` `remainders` (CUBE-root-wide, 2026-11-09) has its products
  and its descent near the crossovers of `fast::mul` and `fast::div_rem` at the sizes of
  `the_cube_of_a_wide_end_scales_with_its_bits`: its widest product is about 550 words at
  2,097,152 bits and 4,000 at 16,777,216. Built alone with 1,088 and 8,051 moduli, the product
  tree's bytes grow 16.1 times and the descent's 15.0 times for 7.7 times the width, while
  the rest of the cube grows 9.8 times. The cube's bytes from 2,097,152 to 16,777,216 bits
  grow 9.92 times (limit 10.06). From 262,144 to 2,097,152 they grow 10.71 times (limit
  10.27): there the tree's top division changes from long division to the reciprocal, and
  dhat (before `num::rem_uint`) put the tree's bytes at 0.39 and 8.95 MB, 23 times, against
  9.46 times for the rest. The instructions pass at both (9.35 and 9.50 times, glibc's
  per-thread cache off). Neither pair is in the test.
- Printing by halves is slower than num-bigint's from about 1024 to 131072 words, with its
  peak at 16384, the same shape as division's, which each level of it calls (the link is
  inferred). Nothing switches back to num-bigint in that range.
- num-bigint 0.4.8 divides above 64 words by Burnikel and Ziegler's recursion over Toom-3
  (`biguint/division.rs` lines 216 and 343) and prints by halves over that division
  (`biguint/convert.rs` line 705), both about `n^1.46`: over these sizes its division grows 24
  times per 8 times the size and its printing 22 times. This is why num-bigint's division and
  printing pass the scaling tests' limit of 24 (merge check: 21.71 and 22.48), and only its gcd
  (Stein's, O(n^2)) fails it.
- The crossings move with the load: the timings of 2026-11-05, at load 45 to 75, put
  multiplication's at 1024 words, the gcd's at 512 to 1024 and printing's break-even at
  262,144; at load 1 they are about 4096, 300 and 131,072.

### KERNEL-leaf-digits, `zed-kernel/src/num/fast.rs` `LEAF_DIGITS` (in `num.rs` until S1F-num-cycle), measured 2026-11-07

`read_digits` reads a text of at most `LEAF_DIGITS` digits whole, O(n^2) (by num-bigint's `parse` when measured; since SWAR-read-literals by `digit_text::read_whole`, K105),
and splits a longer one by halves, O(n log^2 n); the value does not depend on the leaf
(`num::tests::the_leaf_does_not_change_the_value`, leaf 1 against `LEAF_DIGITS` and against
num-bigint). Procedure (the test was not committed): the test build (opt-level 2), random
texts, the fewest instructions of 2 to 20 runs at each leaf, load5 28 to 36. Instructions:

| Digits | leaf 32 | 64 | 128 | 256 | 512 | 1024 | 2048 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 94,516 | 73,183 | 62,109 | 56,689 | 52,879 | 47,480 | 47,480 |
| 10^4 | 1.906 M | 1.705 M | 1.597 M | 1.544 M | 1.514 M | 1.511 M | 1.536 M |
| 10^5 | 66.88 M | 64.89 M | 63.80 M | 63.28 M | 62.98 M | 62.96 M | 63.21 M |
| 10^6 | 1,314.2 M | 1,294.4 M | 1,283.4 M | 1,278.2 M | 1,275.3 M | 1,275.1 M | 1,277.6 M |

The leaf is 1024 (it was 512, not measured): fewest, or tied, at every size measured (700 to 10^6
digits) except 1,500, where 2048 reads the text whole for 10% fewer; from 3,000 digits 2048
costs 0.2% to 2.3% more. From 10^4 digits the leaves 256 to 2048 differ by at most 2.2%, since the
widest products dominate. Processor time agreed within its noise at this load. The peak heap
is the same at 512 and 1024 (23.6 bits per digit on 2^16 to 2^22 nines). The full table, with
700, 1,500, 3,000 and 6,000 digits, is in the comment at the site. The references' copy of the reader (`zed/corpus/ref/src/zedrt.rs`, CORPUS-int-cap) has the same leaf; its products are num-bigint's, as the kernel's are below 1024 words, and it was not timed apart. Measured again with the leaf read eight digits a step (EXP-swar-digits, 2026-11-12, the test build, leaves 128 to 4096 at 3,000 to 10^6 digits): 1024 and 2048 are again the fewest, within 1% of each other, so the leaf stays 1024 (K105).

### BIGINT-fast-mul, `zed-kernel/src/num/fast.rs` `mul`, measured 2026-11-07

`mul` hands a product whose narrower factor has at most `MUL_LEAF` = 512 words to num-bigint
(it was 1024). Above that it computes three costs, in units of one word product of
`sparse_mul`, and takes the least: num-bigint's, `TOOM_COST l s^0.465` for `s <= l` words
(`TOOM_COST` = 10.4, `TOOM_POWER` = `log3(5) - 1`); rows over the nonzero words of the
sparser factor; and the transform plan, `TRANSFORM_COST` = 12 per `n log2(n)` over its pieces.
All three give the same product (`products_agree_with_num_bigint_across_the_crossovers`, 416
products across the leaf and both sides of the cost decision, and `num::fast::tests`).

Procedure (the test was not committed): the release test build of `zed-tests`, random dense
factors from a fixed seed, each method timed as the best of 5 runs of 20 ms at each shape,
load average 16 to 41. Calibration: 1.03 ns a word product of `sparse_mul`; the transform
10.8 to 13.1 ns per `n log2(n)` over 512 to 262,144 points (12.2 on average; before this item
23 to 28 at load 45 to 55); num-bigint 9.1 to 13.4 ns per `l s^0.465` from 256 words (10.7 on
average from 1024). Each entry is `mul`'s time over num-bigint's `*` at the same shape; below
1 `mul` is faster, 1.00 where `mul` takes num-bigint's product.

| Shape (words) | 256 to 1536 | 2048 | 2560 | 3072 | 3584 | 4096 | 5120 | 6144 | 8192 | 12288 | 16384 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| balanced, load 16 to 29 | 1.00 | 0.86 | 1.00 | 1.01 to 1.38 | 0.80 | 0.65 | 0.94 | 0.73 | 0.49 | 0.56 | 0.38 |

| Shape (words) | 512 by 65536 | 768 by 65536 | 1024 by 65536 | 2048 by 16384 | 3000 by 9000 | 8192 by 65536 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| unbalanced, load 16 to 29 | 0.99 | 0.84 | 0.77 | 0.69 | 0.76 | 0.44 |

Before the leaf of 512 words, the transform alone took 1.74 times num-bigint's time at 256 by
256 words, 1.30 at 512 by 512, 1.16 at 256 by 65536 and 1.07 at 512 by 65536 (load 34 to 41),
so it is not used at or below 512. Above it num-bigint is still faster at 1536 by 1536 (the
transform 1.23 times slower) and 2560 by 2560 (1.19), just above powers of two of the
transform's points, which `TOOM_COST` gives to num-bigint.

What is not yet understood:
- At 3072 by 3072 words the two computed costs differ by 5% (the transform on 8192 points,
  1.28 M, against 1.34 M), and the transform is taken. Its time is bimodal over repeated runs
  at the same load: about 1370 microseconds (1.01 to 1.03 times num-bigint's 1350) or about
  1880 (1.38). The same 8192-point transform at 4096 by 4096 words is steady at about 1420
  microseconds. The cause is not measured; a candidate is the placement of the three
  residue buffers of 8192 words each (allocation or cache-set effects). This is the largest
  loss measured above the leaf.
- The scaling test `a_dense_product_scales` (8192 to 65536 words) grows 9.5 times in
  instructions against the `n log n` prediction of about 10.7 and Toom-3's 21.

Sites: every product of two big integers in `num.rs`, `zedc-int/src/int.rs` and

### POLY-nf, `zed-kernel/src/poly.rs` `Poly::mul`, cost formulas, 2026-11-12, fitted 2026-11-13

`Poly::mul` took the dense product (Kronecker substitution into one integer, `num::mul_int`),
until POLY-crossover-bench (below), when `L log2 L` was at most `t1 * t2 * w1 * w2`, for L the words of the packed integers, t the
terms and w the coefficient words of each side; else the sparse product (all products, sorted
and merged). Both formulas have unit constants and no timing was taken, so the crossing is
from cost formulas as P9 asks, with the target's constants still to be measured. The results
are identical: `poly::tests::the_dense_and_sparse_products_agree` compares them on
univariate sums of many terms with wide coefficients, with and without a common step between
indices. Since POLY-nf-power, L counts one slot per multiple of the gcd of the index distances
from each side's lowest index, so a homogeneous sum's empty indices cost nothing. Negative control, run once: the sparse product alone fails
`l03_09_egraph::scaling::the_square_of_a_sum_of_k_powers` at 60.7 times the bytes.
Since POLY-nf-sparse-product a third method, the support product, is tried first when the
indices pack: its cost formula is twice one round of each of its two steps at a prime of 1.5 s,
each round `ntt_cost` of its folded words plus the terms it reads, for s the support's size
estimated from 32 sampled pairs (at least t1 + t2 − 1), plus the sampling, 32 (t1 + t2). It
runs when that is below the cheaper of the other two, and gives way to it once the work it has
counted passes that cost. The constants are unit, as above; at k = 256 the test's square of
`(x + y) ^ k + x` takes the support product, whose counted work was about 0.87 M words against
1.07 M for the sparse product. Since POLY-work-250ms the product is charged to the work limit (POLY-nf-work, QUESTIONS A99) in units fitted to the processor time: `SUPPORT` = 2 times what the support product counted, bounded by the cheaper of the other two costs and by what is left of the budget over `SUPPORT`, and when it gives way, the dense cost or the sparse charge (`PAIR` = 8 plus `w1 w2` a pair) before the method runs. Until POLY-crossover-bench the choice between the dense and the sparse product used the unit constants above, and it was misplaced in both directions: measured in instructions by `crossover poly-*` (2026-11-13), univariate sums of one-word coefficients went sparse up to 45 terms each against a crossover at 5 (9.6 times the work at worst), and up to 8 at 4 words against 6; two sums 16 terms of about every `g` indices went sparse from gap 1 against 6 (5.3 times); 2 terms of `w` words went dense from 11 words, while the sparse product does less at every width to 1024 (2.8 times); 8 terms, dense from 4 words against 110 (2.4 times). No single factor on the old formula fits: per shape it ranged from below 0.02 to 16.

Since POLY-crossover-bench (2026-11-13) the dense product is taken when its estimate, `DENSE_COST` + `SLOT_COST` per output slot + `num::mul_cost` of the two packed integers, is at most the sparse product's, `t1 t2` times `PAIR_COST` + `num::mul_cost` of the widest coefficients (`poly::Choice`), all in units of one word product (about 16 instructions). `num::mul_cost` is the estimate `num::mul` chooses its own method by (schoolbook to `MUL_LEAF`, Toom by `TOOM_COST`, the transforms by `transform_plan`), so a packed product of a few words is no longer costed as a transform. The three constants are fitted jointly over six shapes, each run once per constant (`poly-dense 1`, `poly-dense 4`, `poly-gaps 64`, `poly-gaps 16`, `poly-wide 2`, `poly-wide 8`): `PAIR_COST` = 60, `SLOT_COST` = 40, `DENSE_COST` = 700. With them the choice takes at most 1.087 times the less work (`poly-dense 4`, whose fit, `PAIR_COST` 67 to 84, does not meet `poly-dense 1`'s, 48 to 67) on every shape but `poly-wide 8`, which takes 1.30 times at every value of the three: `num::mul_cost` does not count the zero words that packing leaves between slots, so it overcounts the packed product there; counting them would read the factors, `O(L)`, for each choice. Without `DENSE_COST` (two constants) the best joint fit was 1.41. Cost of the choice: two `num::mul_cost` calls, `O(log L)`, beside the plan's `O(t1 + t2)` pass. The dense charge to the work limit now adds the dense product's fixed and per-slot cost the choice counts, at `PAIR` / `PAIR_COST` units of the limit per word product: without it `(x + y) ^ 72 - x`, whose products the new choice makes dense, took 2.1 to 2.4 times its prediction (POLY-nf-work). Tests: `poly::tests::the_choice_of_product_by_shape` (16 dense terms dense, 16 terms 4096 apart sparse, a span past `usize` sparse with no overflow, one term each sparse), `poly::tests::mul_cost_at_its_corners`, `l03_09_egraph::choice` (8, 16 and 32 dense terms of one-word coefficients dense and 2 terms of 16, 128 and 1024 words sparse, each product equal by both methods; the chosen product of two univariate sums of 1000 and 8000 terms, 12.35 M and 107.45 M instructions, 8.7 times, 0.78 MB and 6.28 MB, 8.0 times, limit 13). Negative control, run once, not committed: with the old choice both shape tests of `l03_09_egraph::choice` fail (8 terms; 16 words).

### CROSSOVER-bench, every crossover, measured 2026-11-12 and 2026-11-13

Every size threshold that switches between two methods with the same result, and every
constant of a cost model that does, now has a benchmark in the binary `crossover` (crate
zed-benches, `benches/`; its module comment lists them). `crossover all` runs each in a process
of its own under 60 s, prints its table, and lists each threshold as built against its measured
crossover and each cost constant against the values that fit all its benchmarks; it exits with
status 1 when one has moved by more than the spread of repeated runs. To repeat:
`zrun systemd-run --user --scope --slice=zedtests.slice -q timeout 75
build/cargo/debug/crossover all` after `zcargo build -p zed-benches --bin crossover`. Work is
counted in instructions (`zed_tests::scaling::Meter`, the least of three runs), in the `dev`
build the tests use; bytes are printed beside them. The thresholds are this platform's
(x86_64-linux, load 33 to 58); the benchmark is run on each target platform on real hardware
and again after any change to either method or to the code generation, and each threshold it
reports moved is reset.

How a threshold is judged (DESIGN.md sec:plan, CROSSOVER-bench). At each size measured the
method the build takes is compared with the method the measured crossover would take; sizes
within 2% of the measured crossover are skipped, since the two methods there differ by less
than the counts vary. The threshold holds when the worst ratio of the work taken over the less
of the two is at most the spread, the most of three runs over the least at any size. For a
setting (a leaf read at several sizes at once) the measure is the sum over the sizes of each
setting's work over the least at that size. A cost constant `C` decides at each input by
comparing `C` times a formula with another cost; each input has the value of `C` at which the
choice flips, so the worst work over all values of `C` is a step function. The steps of every
benchmark of one constant are joined, the worst taken at each value, and the constant is set
inside the range whose worst is least (rounded to two digits); it holds when the work as built
is at most that least worst times the spread.

Measured crossovers against the old values. Repeated runs of `crossover all` gave the same
counts; the spread of three runs at one size is at most 1.0340 (`leaf-digits`), and 1.0187
elsewhere. Last run 2026-11-13, load 37 to 52, and again with the 18 polynomial rows of
POLY-crossover-bench (40 rows), load 45 to 55: every row at its crossover, every constant at
its fit, exit status 0.

With the values now built every row and every constant holds. The worst work left is that of
the cost models themselves: `DIV_COST` 1.089 times the less work (`div-leaf 1 1` asks for 10.6
to 11.9 and `div-leaf 256 1` for 7.7 to 8.2; `1 4` 10.4 to 10.5, `4 1` 9.06 to 9.22, `16 1`
9.0 to 10.0), `TOOM_COST` 1.047 (`mul 4` against `mul 1`), and `Poly::mul`'s three constants
1.087 (`poly-dense 4` against `poly-dense 1`) and 1.30 on `poly-wide 8` at any value (the
POLY-nf section); a better model, not another
constant, would lower them. The kernel `LEAF_DIGITS` stays at 1024: at 2048 the sum over its
sizes is 1.0279 times less, within its spread of 1.0340.

Division. A leaf on the narrower of the quotient and the divisor cannot sit at every crossover:
num-bigint's division does less work up to 3192 words for `2w` by `w` and only up to 242 for a
quotient 256 times the divisor, so any one leaf lost at least 1.39 times on one shape.
`div_rem` now keeps num-bigint's division past `DIV_LEAF` wherever its computed cost is at most
the cheaper of the other two methods', as `mul` does with `TOOM_COST`: `DIV_COST s^1.52 (s +
wider)` / `s` for the narrower `s` of the quotient's and divisor's words and `wider` the other's
words beyond `s` (times 0.45 when the divisor is the wider), fitted to num-bigint's measured
work (2.79 to 2.90 times per doubling of `2w` by `w`, `2^1.52`; within about 3% at the shapes
measured). A `Divisor` used many times (`div_rem_blocks`, printing, the remainder tree) now
makes the choice `div_rem` makes for its whole quotient, by the same costs. Before, it chose for
one division of `2 len` words with no num-bigint past `DIV_LEAF`, and a quotient of 256 times
the divisor's words went by long division from 91 to 235 words, 1.9 to 2.6 times num-bigint's
work. `print-whole` and the wide `div-leaf` shapes measure it.

size of some scaling pairs than at the larger, which raises their ratios. Under the limit of 13
at 8n (TESTS-scaling-limit-13) three of the `l01_18_scalar_interpreter::scaling` pairs that
rose keep their sizes; one moved. Ratios of the work, 2026-11-13, load 37:

| reading an int of n digits | 160,000 | 12.0 | 11.94 |
| reading a rat of n digits (three texts) | 160,000 | not recorded | 11.57 to 11.88 |
| reading a rat of two wide parts | 80,000 | 12.3 (bytes 11.6) | 12.37 (bytes 12.06) |
| reading a decimal with powers of 2 and 5 (eight texts) | 160,000, now 640,000 | not recorded | 10.63 to 11.19 (bytes 8.85 to 9.58) |

At 160,000 the family with high powers of 2 and 5 took 14.8 times the work in its first runs,
which the limit holds too, from divisions by a power of 5 of 75 to 1189 words that num-bigint
does at both sizes. The decimals now run at 640,000 and 5,120,000 digits as four tests, one a
family, so that libtest runs them at once (`reading_a_decimal_with_a_high_power_of_5_scales`,
`..._a_high_power_of_2_...`, `..._high_powers_of_2_and_5_...`, `..._no_high_power_...`). The
step's tests take 17 s at load 37. Under the limit of 10.5 (TESTS-scaling-limit-10_5) all seven
of these tests are over the limit and are ignored with the row RADIX-nlog2-10_5.

`l01_24_refinement_lattices::scaling::the_cube_of_a_wide_end_scales_with_its_bits` now checks
4,096 and 32,768 bits and 131,072 and 1,048,576. The remainder tree's first division, of the end
by the product of the filter primes (37 words at 32,768 bits, 80 at 131,072, 477 at 1,048,576),
crosses `DIV_LEAF` between 32,768 and 262,144 bits. Past the leaf `DIV_COST` hands it to
num-bigint's Burnikel–Ziegler division. At 262,144 bits that does 12% less work than the
reciprocal but allocates 1.69 times the bytes, so the old second pair grew 14.6 times in bytes,
over the limit of 13. From 131,072 bits both runs are past the leaf: 8.5 times the work and 7.7 the
bytes. No pair past the leaf keeps that division on one side of `DIV_COST`'s crossover, since
the product grows about 6 times for 8 times the bits; at the crossover the two methods do equal
work, so crossing it changes the ratio little.

Tests that follow a threshold rather than a written number: `l01_24 num_text` computes the
handoff leaf and first power from `PRINT_HANDOFF`; `m0_04 int_reading` reads the corpus
`LEAF_DIGITS`. `zed-kernel`'s unit tests keep `DIV_COST`, `TOOM_COST` and the leaves at their
test values (infinite or small), so that both sides of each are reached; the benchmark checks
every method against the other for equal output at every size it measures.

Not benchmarked. `Pairs::meets`'s `l * r <= 1` and `Pairs::tried`'s `l n <= 16 (l + n)` in
`zedc-types` `ty.rs` (F132) switch between filing and scanning inside the type checker, whose
cost depends on how many pairs meet and is reached only through a checked program, not through
an operation the binary can call; both are measured at their sites over 72 cases and are to be
measured again at the Zed port. `SPARSE_STEP` (20) is not fitted: the divisors of `div-rows`
have too few nonzero words for its share to show. The support product's cost formula in `Poly::mul` (`poly.rs`, POLY-nf-sparse-product) keeps
unit constants: `poly::crossover` exposes the dense and the sparse product and the value of each
fitted constant at which the choice between them flips, not the support product.

Negative control, run once and not committed (2026-11-13, load 183 from other builds; the
counts are instructions and do not depend on it): with `GCD_LEAF` set to 2048 words,
`crossover all` exits with status 1 and reports `gcd-leaf` MOVED, 2.18 times the least work at
2048 words against the measured 300; every other row stays at its crossover. Restored to 299.

## Kept

| Where | Why |
|---|---|
| Fourier–Motzkin pairs | an elimination runs only while it adds no terms to the rows (DESIGN L1.38), so the pairs of one elimination are at most the rows it removes times the rows it adds back, and the rows never grow; a system needing a growing elimination is refused (Growth). Since Q1-LOCAL an exact elimination whose count per row shows growth is still taken when the rows it writes, counted after cancellation and against the rows held, add no terms (row Q1-LOCAL), and a row of two terms implied strictly by another over the same pair within the bounds is not kept |
| undeclared parameters (check), `apply` | each body checked once; a class is merged or loses a carrier at most (values + 6 × classes) times, each step O(log N) by union by rank, so O(N log N); an application over unions keeps one state per set of arrows still alive, at most 2^(A+1) for an operator of A arrows, a constant of the prelude, so it is linear in the parts of its arguments. The search this replaced (RUNS, CONTEXTS, COMBOS, F6, F18) was exponential and capped. A literal joins its class by one find, O(log N): a plain one keeps only its own carrier, and where a type does not hold that carrier the menu names at most three forms (LIT-plain, 2026-11-05); `fewest` reads each arrow of a call once against each argument, O(A × the size of the arguments) |
| emptiness and subtyping of tuple and morphism parts (`types/bdd.rs`, `types/empty.rs`) | deciding emptiness of a Boolean combination of tuple or morphism types is coNP-hard, so `is_empty` is sound and not complete (`Type::verdict` names each refusal: Fork, a recursive component two tuple types differ in, or two recursive types on a cycle taken out of one component, the subset construction (`is_empty` counts it inhabited); Residues, the NP-hard covering problem for residues, one prime split at a time; TupleSplit; MorphismSplit, one split into morphism types per branch; NoWitness; each has a Complexity tradeoff comment at its site in `types/empty.rs` and a case in `l01_23_subtyping::refusals::each_refusal_names_its_cause`): it never calls an inhabited type empty, but a part that only a split of the box in two or more components at once proves empty counts as inhabited, and a subtyping check that needs it fails with an error naming the types (the Complexity tradeoff comment in `types/empty.rs`; `l01_23_subtyping::scaling::a_type_not_proved_empty_promises_no_key`, four pigeons in three holes). No count stops the check (docs/thresholds.md 9; memory one path and one split at a time). A diagram has no more nodes than its operands together, so none is exponential in what was written; its paths can be, and so can its display (a parity of `C` tuple types has `2^(C-1)` clauses) |
| `zedc::axioms::of` and the M0.11 harness check of the order axioms (AXIOMS-order) | `of` filters the constant table `AXIOMS` (137 entries since FLOAT-minmax), whose size the language fixes and no program changes, so a lookup is O(1) in the program. The harness checks `Implies` on the pairs and `Composes` on the triples of a fixed instance set (17 integers, 9 floats), as `Transitive` already did; it is a test of the table, not of a program, so it has no scaling test. |
| M0.11 harness check of the bit-word axioms, `check_word` and `check_shift` (BIT-axioms) | `check_word` builds the table of `bitAnd`, `bitOr` or `bitXor` on the `w`-digit values, 4^w evaluations, and checks a law with one lookup per tuple: 8^w triples for associativity, 4^w pairs, 2^w singles, so the work is linear in the tuples checked. `check_shift` evaluates two terms per pair (`x`, `k`). `m0_11_prelude_axioms_and_limits::scaling::the_harness_is_linear_in_the_tuples_it_checks`: associativity of `bitXor` at 8^6 and 8^7 triples, power 1. |
| `min` and `max` on floats: `value::ieee_min_max` (in `eval.rs` until MINMAX-tuples moved it, so `value.rs` does not import `eval.rs`) and the code generator's inline `fmin`/`fmax` (FLOAT-minmax) | one comparison and at most one sign test per call, O(1); native code runs them inline with no kernel call, so a program's work in them is linear in the calls. `l01_36_cranelift::minmax::a_fold_of_min_scales_linearly`: a fold of `min` over 1,000 and 8,000 floats compiled and run natively, 64,650,566 and 529,608,554 bytes (8.2x, limit 24 for linear work), load 52 to 53. Negative control, run once: a fold made quadratic was refuted at 32.4x. |
| `zed_tests::scaling` `Meter::first_that_moves`, `one_test_at_a_time`, `zed_alloc_count::os` (PERF-portable) | `first_that_moves` reads a fixed list of at most two counters, each over 100,000 passes of a constant loop; `one_test_at_a_time` reads the test binary's arguments once, linear in their number; each `os` call is one system call. None depends on a program's size, so they have no scaling test; their unit tests are in `scaling.rs`. |
| `zed_alloc_count` `count`, the walk up the chain of threads at each allocation (WRITE-prefix-scale; SCALE-threads made the chain) | on Linux each allocation adds its bytes to the count of its thread and of every thread in the chain that started it, O(d) per allocation for a chain d threads long. Test binaries and the `zedc` executable (for `zedc --report`, through `zed-native`; corrected by KERNEL-alloc-count-cost, which read "only test binaries") use this allocator, and the compiler and runtime start no threads (every `spawn` in `crates/` is in a test), so d is set by a test's own code: the harness's thread for the test, the thread of each run (`scaling::alone`) and the threads a test starts, about three, and no program's size changes it. Keeping one count per thread and summing a thread's descendants at each read would make a read O(threads) and need the live threads listed; the walk is the cheaper side. Tests `zed_alloc_count::tests::a_thread_counts_in_the_count_of_the_thread_that_started_it`. |
| `zed_alloc_count` `Counting` (`alloc`, `alloc_zeroed`, `realloc`, `dealloc`) and the cfg(test) `hash::salted` in `zed-kernel` (KERNEL-alloc-count-cost) | the same order, O(1) per call plus the walk of the row above; a smaller constant. The three thread-locals the allocator read (the chain's count, the thread's own bytes, the measurement's net and peak) are one `const`-initialized thread-local, read once per call, so `dealloc` with no measurement running reads one flag. `salted` read `SALT` through `LocalKey::get`, which std does not mark inline, so each `mix` made an out-of-line call through a pointer; `try_with`, which std marks inline, makes it one `xor` with a `%fs` load. Callgrind on `types::bdd::tests::parity_built_a_literal_at_a_time_scales`: 33.51 G instructions before, 31.17 G after (7.0% fewer); `mix` with the salt read 39 to 19 instructions per call (the salt read was 6.0% of the test); the allocator's own code and the `__rust_*` shims 5.73% to 5.07% of the test (alloc 45.9 to 40.9 per call; dealloc with its shim 31.0 to 21.0). What `alloc` keeps is the call to malloc, the walk up the chain (one `lock add` per thread) and the measurement flag. Counts stay exact: `a_fixed_workload_counts_its_bytes_exactly` and `..._on_each_of_many_threads` (8 threads, 10 runs each) check the bytes, the net and the peak of a fixed workload; negative control (run once, not committed): `alloc_zeroed` counting 0 bytes fails them, 8,010 counted against 58,510. Each scaling test of `zed-kernel` (55 ratios) and three of l01_22 and l01_28 run alone on both builds: every instruction ratio within 0.7% of main's, most within 0.2%. |
| `zed-kernel` `local::with` and its callers: `deep::free_in`, `Literal::table` of `Row` and `Morphism` (`TUPLES`, `MORPHISMS`), `Shared::new`, `Type::empty`, `top`, the scalars, `universe`, `zip_at_once`, `value::fresh_id` (KERNEL-tls-inline) | the same order, O(1) per read; a smaller constant. std's `LocalKey::with` is not marked inline, so each instance is compiled in one code unit of the crate and every other unit calls it, with the closure inside; `local::with` reads through `try_with`, which std marks inline, so the read is compiled into its caller, and it panics with `with`'s message when the thread-local is gone. Instructions (perf stat, repeat runs within 0.001%): `types::bdd::tests::parity_built_a_literal_at_a_time_scales` 31.167 G to 30.452 G (2.29% fewer; the tuple tables 1.49%, the type drop queue 0.79%, the other sites 0.02%); l01_22 `kinds::the_difference_of_many_wide_tuple_types_scales` 4.142 G to 4.114 G (0.68%) and `kinds::meets_of_many_tuples_scales` 1.876 G to 1.863 G (0.68%). Left: `__tls_get_addr`, 0.7 to 0.9% of the l01_22 and l01_39 tests, the cost of a thread-local in a shared library (the test build links `zed-kernel` as one), which inlining does not remove. |

Each law is read with `!` moved onto the comparisons (`==` and `!=` swap) and `(a).implies(b)` as `!a \|\| b`, then put in conjunctive normal form (C32 (2)). A clause of one comparison is a constraint: when its sides name no common field, two constraints joined by a hidden end symbol, O(p log p) for p paths; otherwise the pairs of paths that agree, numbered and written as runs of pair numbers (C32 (1)). A clause of several comparisons is checked when one of its fields becomes fixed and at most one is then open, with a union-find with parities over #a, #b and the binders, O(c log c) for c comparisons; with one field f open, the comparisons that do not reach f are related once, and each live choice of f relates only the comparisons that reach f, from f's call on (each such comparison holds f's call with all its arguments, so this is linear in the clause, not the choices times the clause). Arc consistency is incremental: counts of live cubes per choice, per variable of a constraint and per constraint, the variables of a constraint kept ordered by how many live cubes mention them, so a choice left unsupported is found without a scan, and each cube is removed at most once per descent; an atom held as pairs keeps, for each choice of each variable, the list of runs of the pairs that use it and one list of the pairs that do not mention the variable, each list watching its first live pair, over a set of live pairs that gives the next live one in O(log p), so each pair is removed and each list's runs are passed at most once per descent; a depth-first search in declaration order undoes by a trail. The default report lists at most two models per group and stops at the first choice that leads to no model, so it does O(size of the group's laws) work per choice and at most one choice per field before it ends; `@exhaustive` lists every model, at work proportional to the models listed on groups whose laws are atoms or conjunctions of atoms and whose field-atom graph is a forest (no choice there leads to no model, `brute::the_report_agrees_with_brute_force_on_random_theories`, 1,215 such theories, 0 dead ends), and exponential in the fields elsewhere, where deciding that a model exists is NP-complete (`hardness`) | tests `l22_08_vacuity::scaling`, k = 1,000 and 8,000 fields, limit 11.4 (the n log n limit since SCALE-ratio; 24 when first measured), instructions and bytes: free fields 7.7 and 8.1 times, codecs side by side 8.0 and 8.0, a chain of equations 8.0 and 8.0 (default) and 8.0 and 8.1 (`@exhaustive`), small groups 8.0 and 8.0, one group of 2^(k+1) models (`star`, default report) 8.0 and 8.0, the split alone 8.0 and 8.0, random 3-CNF at 4.26 clauses per variable (default report) 8.0 and 8.0, one atom between two balanced trees of k/2 fields each 8.9 and 9.3 (each path holds about log k choices; 3,436,911 and 31,986,695 bytes. It was 11.5, 7,475,983 and 86,242,583 bytes, until the engine's tables were made at their final lengths, the cubes that use a choice kept in one array with offsets and a split atom's paths moved rather than copied twice: by phase the engine's tables grew 12.1 times through doubling, the written paths 10.4 times), one `\|\|` of k - 1 comparisons 8.3 and 8.5, one `\|\|` whose last field has k/2 arguments (`one_wide_field_scales`) 8.3 and 8.4; load1 14 to 35. A law is parsed with binders and fields looked up by hash map, O(1) per name (a scan per name was quadratic, found by `hardness::the_work_limit_is_not_a_size_limit`). | NARROW-ne-rat-divisor | a `rat` divisor the tests it is under keep from `0r` (NARROW-ne-rat-divisor, DESIGN.md sec:type_resolution on a divisor that holds no zero): `nonzero` in `Ck::binary_op` reading `Ck::may_be_here` of a `rat` divisor, `Ck::term` reading `rat` literals (`Ck::rat_literal`) and a literal with no suffix at the carrier it adopts (`Ck::carrier_here`), all in `crates/zedc-check/src/check/walk.rs`; the comparison of a name with a `rat` literal in `Scope::atom_names`, `crates/zedc-preimage/src/product.rs` | A division by a `rat` whose type holds `0r` reads the divisor's product in the scope of its arm once, as an `int` divisor reads its integers (row NARROW-ne-divisor): one settle and one forward evaluation. A comparison `r < q`, `r <= q`, `r > q`, `r >= q` with a `rat` literal `q` reads the sign of `q` once and, where `0r` fails the comparison in the arm, meets `r` with the complement of `0r`, O(1) a test. The full method, an interval domain over `rat` names beside the integer one, would narrow `r > 1r { x / (r - 1r) }` too, at the cost of a second abstract domain in the reduced product; only the zero exclusion is needed for `#divByZero`. Reading a literal's carrier is one lookup of its adopted value (`info.adopt`) or of the class mask of the expression's type | Test `l01_26_type_resolution::divisors::chained_rat_tests_and_divisions_check_in_linear_time` (n = 100 and 800 chained tests, in turn `r != 0r`, `r >= 1r` and `r != 0`, each with a division by `r` in its arm): 7.98 times the work and 7.98 times the bytes (load 23), limit 13. Negative control, run once and not committed: the check run m/100 times at size m, 63.9 times the bytes, failed |
| PORT-out-param | output ports passed to functions (PORT-out-param; DESIGN.md L1.19): `ports` in `crates/zedc-check/src/check/ports.rs`, called from `check_with` in `check/walk.rs`; `Builder::passed` in `crates/zedc-syntax/src/ast/builder.rs`; `State::push` in `crates/zedc-elab/src/elab/state.rs` | Which parameters are output ports: the parameters pushed to seed a worklist, and one backward search over the edges "parameter passed whole → parameter it fills" adds the rest, each parameter entering once through a visited set, O(P + A) for P parameters and A arguments; every use of a port is then checked by one lookup, O(U) for U uses. The naive method, a search of the calls for each parameter found, is O(P · A), quadratic on a chain of helpers. `Builder::passed` maps each call argument's inner span to the whole argument in one walk of the tree, kept once made, so each `m.stdout` asks O(1), where a search up from the use for each one costs the depth. A push to a parameter becomes a choice over `main`'s output ports, at most 2, O(1) a push; copying each function once per port it is given (specialization) would cost P^k copies for k nested helpers | Test `l01_19_whole_file_ports::ports::a_chain_of_helpers_passing_a_port_scales` (the pass alone over a chain of n helpers, n = 1,000 and 8,000): 8.1 times the instructions and 8.0 times the bytes, limit 13. Negative control, run once and not committed: a scan of every call for each parameter found, 19.8 times the work, failed. Timing the whole check instead hid the same control (8.7 times), since the pass is a small part of it |

Here one trial of the application per piece of the type (a carrier, the other scalars, a tuple shape, a function), atoms and text taken out, stopping at the first piece taken: O(p) trials for p pieces | Test `l01_29_diagnostics::scaling::a_text_repair_of_many_shapes_scales`: a union of tuples of every length to k, about 800 and 6,400 components (k = 40 and 113), 5.9 times the instructions and 5.3 times the bytes (6.3 without the trials); limit 13. A trial costs about the same at both sizes, as types are shared. Negative control (not committed): each trial also writes out the whole type, O(n^1.5), 21.7 times the bytes |
| S-sched | the scheduler of a build's checks, evaluations and compilations (SCHED-dep-dag; DESIGN.md sec:checking_in_zed, "Checks and evaluations on one dependency graph"): `Schedule::demand` and `Schedule::run` in `crates/zedc-lattice/src/schedule.rs`, re-exported as `zedc::store::schedule` | Naive: rounds over all nodes until nothing changes, O(k (n + e)) for k rounds with k up to n, re-running a once node (a verdict, an evaluation) from its start each time it meets a value not yet final, O(k²) polls for a node of k reads. Here one depth-first search in Tarjan's manner (Tarjan 1972): each node entered once, each read answered once, a once node polled once per read, O(n + e); each component of iterable nodes solved once, O((n_C + e_C) · h); a refused component costs one breadth-first search inside it, and the parent marks are reset over its members only, so all refusals together cost O(n + e). Four 32-bit words per node besides its value | Test `m0_05_widening_and_iteration::schedule::scaling`: 4,000 and 32,000 groups (about 14,700 and 118,000 nodes), each a two-node iterable component reading the previous group's and a check reading it and the previous check, every seventh group a refused pair of once nodes and a definition reading them, and one refused ring of n / 4 once nodes, demanded from the last node so the search runs n groups deep; 7.96 times the instructions and 8.00 times the bytes; limit 10.5. Negative control (not committed): the refusal resets the parent marks over every node instead of the component's members, O(n) per refusal and n/7 refusals, 29.2 times the instructions. The declarative rounds the test compares the engine with (`reference`) took 43.2 times the bytes at 40 and 320 nodes (its closure is an n × n matrix) |
